claims.text: Adding a small amount of silicon to ZrB2 will enable densification at temperatures below 1700 °C.
Silicon promotes grain-boundary liquid-phase formation during sintering.
Silicon segregates to grain boundaries in the processed ZrB2 body.
Segregated silicon develops an amorphous Si–B–O or silicate layer at grain boundaries during service.
Lower-temperature liquid-phase sintering produces a dense, well-bonded ZrB2 microstructure.
In high-temperature oxidative environments, segregated silicon forms an adherent protective silicate glass.
The protective silicate glass inhibits oxygen ingress.
The protective silicate glass inhibits corrosion by liquid plating metals.
Silicon-doped ZrB2 made below 1700 °C will have strength and structural integrity comparable to or greater than single-phase ZrB2 made above 2300 °C.
Silicon-doped ZrB2 will have significantly better oxidation resistance than both high-temperature-sintered single-phase ZrB2 and previously reported lower-temperature specimens.
Silicon-doped ZrB2 will undergo less liquid plating-metal corrosion than both high-temperature-sintered single-phase ZrB2 and previously reported lower-temperature specimens.
Previously reported lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens have inadequate oxidation resistance.
Previously reported lower-temperature ZrB2 specimens have inadequate liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
The proposed intervention uses a silicon concentration tentatively described as a few atomic percent.
The proposed manufacturing boundary is pressureless sintering at or below 1700 °C.
The proposed service boundary includes oxidation above 1200 °C and prolonged exposure to liquid plating-metal baths.
Copper-based baths are an applicable example of the targeted liquid plating-metal environment.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome and falsification rule require comparison with high-temperature-processed ZrB2 and previously reported lower-temperature specimens, but the experimental design explicitly prepares only silicon-doped and undoped specimens processed at or below 1700 °C. Thus, the stated experiment cannot directly evaluate all required baseline comparisons.
